description: CTS Corporation designs, manufactures, and sells sensors, connectivity components, and actuators in North America, Europe, and Asia. The company offers controls, pedals, sensors, switches, transducers
description_full: CTS Corporation designs, manufactures, and sells sensors, connectivity components, and actuators in North America, Europe, and Asia. The company offers controls, pedals, sensors, switches, transducers, and piezo sensing products; EMI/RFI filters, capacitors, resistors, RF filters, and frequency control products; and piezo microactuators and rotary actuators. In addition, it designs, develops, and manufactures advanced pressure sensing technologies for medical devices, life sciences, and industrial applications. It serves transportation, industrial, medical, aerospace, and defense industries. The company sells and markets its products through its sales engineers, independent manufacturer representatives, and distributors. CTS Corporation was founded in 1896 and is headquartered in Lisle, Illinois.
ceo_bio: Mr. Pratik  Trivedi | President, CEO & Director | Age 46 | Compensation: $682,451 (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 3K people. Revenue per employee of $155K ranks in the bottom quartile among Technology peers. Each employee generates $25K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: CTS Corporation is a small-cap technology business with a $1.7B market cap on $541M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 9% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 35%.

The business throws off $86M in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.56× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 19× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.1% of the shares.

Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 8pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.65x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-3.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 33% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 13% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 37% and a beta of 0.98, it moves roughly with the market.
About $11.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 21% in the 2022 bear market and 84% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 29% below its DCF fair value of $85.00, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 55%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $65.99 to $111 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: EV/EBITDA 12.5 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 19.9 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 39% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 5.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $73.67 on average, 22% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 9.5%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.40).
It runs a 35% gross margin and converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow, or 4% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.56x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 4.7% of revenue on R&D and 0.7% on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.4, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.7% over 3 years, 5.0% over 5 years and 3.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.9% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 2% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 23%.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (2.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 9, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (3.3% in buybacks and 0.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, though it has been cut 1.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 3,492 employees, each generates about $155K of revenue, 0.4x the Technology median.
That works out to $25K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $682K (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
